item.title: Optical depth (astrophysics)
item.description:
Optical depth in astrophysics refers to a measure of transparency for electromagnetic radiation within an astrophysical medium. Quantified by the symbol τ, it measures how much a beam of light is attenuated due to absorption and scattering as it travels through a physical distance z. The optical depth at a given frequency ν is defined as the integral of the extinction coefficient αν (the sum of absorption and scattering coefficients) along the radiation path:
τν(z)≡∫0zαν(z′)dz′=σνN, where σν is the extinction cross-section per particle and N is the column density (the number of target particles per unit area along the line of sight). Large values (τν≫1) indicate an optically thick medium with high obscuration, whereas small values (τν≪1) correspond to an optically thin medium where radiation passes through largely unhindered. In radiative transfer, the attenuation of monochromatic intensity Iν along a path is described by the Beer–Lambert law:
Iν(z)=Iν,0e−τν Alternatively, the extinction coefficient α can be related to the imaginary part of the complex refractive index, κ, by:
α=4πκλ0, where λ0 is the vacuum wavelength of the incident light.
